statement: In a given pentagon, which is equilateral and equiangular, to inscribe a circle.
heath_proof: Let ABCDE be the given equilateral and equiangular pentagon; thus it is required to inscribe a circle in the pentagon ABCDE. For let the angles BCD, CDE be bisected by the straight lines CF, DF respectively; and from the point F, at which the straight lines CF, DF meet one another, let the straight lines FB, FA, FE be joined. Then, since BC is equal to CD, and CF common, the two sides BC, CF are equal to the two sides DC, CF; and the angle BCF is equal to the angle DCF; therefore the base BF is equal to the base DF, and the triangle BCF is equal to the triangle DCF, and the remaining angles will be equal to the remaining angles, namely those which the equal sides subtend. [I. 4] Therefore the angle CBF is equal to the angle CDF. And, since the angle CDE is double of the angle CDF, and the angle CDE is equal to the angle ABC, while the angle CDF is equal to the angle CBF; therefore the angle CBA is also double of the angle CBF; therefore the angle ABF is equal to the angle FBC; therefore the angle ABC has been bisected by the straight line BF. Similarly it can be proved that the angles BAE, AED have also been bisected by the straight lines FA, FE respectively. Now let FG, FH, FK, FL, FM be drawn from the point F perpendicular to the straight lines AB, BC, CD, DE, EA. Then, since the angle HCF is equal to the angle KCF, and the right angle FHC is also equal to the angle FKC, FHC, FKC are two triangles having two angles equal to two angles and one side equal to one side, namely FC which is common to them and subtends one of the equal angles; therefore they will also have the remaining sides equal to the remaining sides; [I. 26] therefore the perpendicular FH is equal to the perpendicular FK. Similarly it can be proved that each of the straight lines FL, FM, FG is also equal to each of the straight lines FH, FK; therefore the five straight lines FG, FH, FK, FL, FM are equal to one another. Therefore the circle described with centre F and distance one of the straight lines FG, FH, FK, FL, FM will pass also through the remaining points; and it will touch the straight lines AB, BC, CD, DE, EA, because the angles at the points G, H, K, L, M are right. For, if it does not touch them. but cuts them, it will result that the straight line drawn at right angles to the diameter of the circle from its extremity falls within the circle: which was proved absurd. [III. 16] Therefore the circle described with centre F and distance one of the straight lines FG, FH, FK, FL, FM will not cut the straight lines AB, BC, CD, DE, EA; therefore it will touch them. Let it be described, as GHKLM. Therefore in the given pentagon, which is equilateral and equiangular, a circle has been inscribed.

**Step 2.** Bisect angle BCD by the straight line CF, and bisect angle CDE by the straight line DF, where F is the point at which CF and DF meet [1.9, P1].

**Step 3.** Join FB, FA, and FE [P1].

**Step 4.** Since BC equals CD (the pentagon is equilateral), CF is common, and angle BCF equals angle DCF (CF bisects angle BCD), triangles BCF and DCF are congruent by SAS [1.4]. Therefore BF equals DF, and angle CBF equals angle CDF.

**Step 5.** Now angle CDF equals half of angle CDE (since DF bisects angle CDE). Since the pentagon is equiangular, angle ABC equals angle CDE, so half of angle ABC equals half of angle CDE. From Step 4, angle CBF equals angle CDF, which equals half of angle CDE, which equals half of angle ABC. Therefore angle CBF equals half of angle ABC, and so BF bisects angle ABC.

**Step 6.** Since CD equals DE (equilateral pentagon), DF is common, and angle CDF equals angle EDF (DF bisects angle CDE), triangles CDF and EDF are congruent by SAS [1.4]. Therefore CF equals EF, and angle DCF equals angle DEF.

**Step 7.** Now angle DCF equals half of angle BCD (since CF bisects angle BCD). Since the pentagon is equiangular, angle DEA equals angle BCD, so half of angle DEA equals half of angle BCD. From Step 6, angle DEF equals angle DCF, which equals half of angle BCD, which equals half of angle DEA. Therefore angle DEF equals half of angle DEA, and so EF bisects angle DEA.

**Step 8.** From F, draw FG perpendicular to AB, FH perpendicular to BC, FK perpendicular to CD, FL perpendicular to DE, and FM perpendicular to EA [1.12].

**Step 9.** In triangles FHC and FKC: CF is common, angle HCF equals angle KCF (since CF bisects angle BCD), and angle FHC equals angle FKC (both being right angles) [P4]. By AAS, triangles FHC and FKC are congruent [1.26]. Therefore FH equals FK.

**Step 10.** In triangles FKD and FLD: DF is common, angle KDF equals angle LDF (since DF bisects angle CDE), and angle FKD equals angle FLD (both being right angles) [P4]. By AAS, triangles FKD and FLD are congruent [1.26]. Therefore FK equals FL.

**Step 11.** In triangles FHB and FGB: BF is common, angle HBF equals angle GBF (since BF bisects angle ABC, as shown in Step 5), and angle FHB equals angle FGB (both being right angles) [P4]. By AAS, triangles FHB and FGB are congruent [1.26]. Therefore FH equals FG.

**Step 12.** In triangles FLE and FME: EF is common, angle LEF equals angle MEF (since EF bisects angle DEA, as shown in Step 7), and angle FLE equals angle FME (both being right angles) [P4]. By AAS, triangles FLE and FME are congruent [1.26]. Therefore FL equals FM.

**Step 13.** From Steps 9 through 12: FG equals FH (Step 11), FH equals FK (Step 9), FK equals FL (Step 10), and FL equals FM (Step 12). Therefore FG equals FH equals FK equals FL equals FM [CN1].

**Step 14.** Describe the circle GHKLM with center F and radius FG [P3]. This circle passes through H, K, L, and M as well, since FG equals FH equals FK equals FL equals FM.

**Step 15.** Since FG is perpendicular to AB and FG is a radius of circle GHKLM, the circle meets AB at G and does not cut it; that is, AB is tangent to the circle at G [3.16]. By the same reasoning, BC is tangent to the circle at H, CD is tangent at K, DE is tangent at L, and EA is tangent at M.

**Step 16.** Therefore the circle GHKLM is inscribed in the pentagon ABCDE, since each side of the pentagon touches the circle [D4.5].

Therefore, in the given equilateral and equiangular pentagon, a circle has been inscribed, which is what was required to do.
